turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Thursday, the first of October. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
[curious] Moscow put a nuclear threat to NATO in writing this week. The man it was addressed to says he doesn't take it seriously.
[curious] The Secretary General said that? Out loud?
Out loud, on the record, the same day.
[wry] Right. And here at home, two household bills moved on Tuesday in opposite directions — and the same barrel of oil set both of them.
And Pakistan's regulator tried to stop the middle class free-riding on the grid, and accidentally made a battery worth four times a grid connection. [wry] That one's the long read.
Let's start in Brussels.
[amused] On Wednesday a Russian non-paper reached NATO headquarters. A non-paper is an unsigned, deniable note — the lowest-commitment object in the whole diplomatic repertoire.
So what did it say?

[deadpan] That Russia will be ready to use, quote, the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, if NATO attempts isolating the Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country.
[pause] And that's new?
[warmly] The words aren't. Moscow has said versions of that aloud for years. The delivery is new. A written state communication, threatening nuclear use against European territory.
Okay. That's a sentence I'd like to sit with for a second.
[skeptical] There's one clause with no prior public equivalent. That a conflict could include strikes against decision-making centres in alliance member states, right from the outset.
[thoughtful] So why is the desk's headline that nobody's taking it seriously?

[chuckles] Because the people best placed to take it seriously aren't. Mark Rutte, on the record: I don't take this seriously. He declined to confirm the contents at all and suggested Moscow publish them itself.
That's a striking thing for the target of a nuclear threat to say.
[thoughtful] Lithuania's even blunter. Their president's security adviser called the threats completely baseless, and a measure of psychological pressure.
And Lithuania is the one who'd actually have to do the blockading.
[curious] Lithuania is the one. Sixty-five kilometres of Polish-Lithuanian corridor separates Kaliningrad from Belarus. Any isolation happens there or nowhere.
So there's a plan Russia is threatening to retaliate against.
[deadpan] That's the thing. There isn't one. Nothing in the public record describes a plan to isolate Kaliningrad. Russia is promising to retaliate for a contingency it has largely constructed.
[laughs] Oh, that's good. That's genuinely good.

[wry] And here's the honest caveat, which we're printing prominently. The document is not public. One news agency has seen it. Every account in circulation — ours included — is an account of their reading of it.
Which means what, exactly, for a listener?
[amused] It means a non-paper is unsigned by definition. Its provenance, and whether it was authorised at political level, are both unverified.
Mm.
[deadpan] What would falsify the story: near-identical language turning up in an earlier note. That would make Wednesday a reporting event and not a policy event.
There's one more thing on that page I liked, which is an absence.

[warmly] Xinhua and CGTN carried no Kaliningrad item from the twenty-ninth of September to the first of October. Their world files led on Iran and Iraq. The story that took the European wires simply did not run.
Money block. Talk to me about Wednesday.

[skeptical] Wednesday ran a clean experiment. Half past eight in Washington, the August personal-income release. Core inflation came in at zero point two per cent on the month and three point oh on the year — against a consensus of zero point three and three point three.
So softer than expected on both.
[chuckles] On both. And the odds of an October rate rise fell from about seventy per cent to thirty-nine.
Wait — really?
[thoughtful] The ten-year rose to five point two nine per cent. The thirty-year to five point six four. Both are twenty-twenty-six highs.
So the bond market got handed good news about the Fed, and sold anyway.
[curious] Both ends of the curve rose, and the long end rose faster. That's called a bear steepener. It's what a market does when it wants paying to hold time, rather than to hold policy risk.
And the front end?
[wry] Did the opposite. The three-month actually fell five basis points, pricing the easier Fed. The distance between those two behaviours is term premium, and it widened all week.
Give me one number I can hold.
The twenty-year now yields more than the thirty. Five point six eight against five point six four.
That's backwards.
It's backwards, and it's held on sixty-one of a hundred and eighty-eight sessions this year. It's a supply fingerprint at the very long end. Not a macro signal.
[curious] And the desk argues against itself on this one, doesn't it?
It does, and the third objection is the serious one. The equity market disagrees — and the equity market holds the cash flows.
Go on.

In a genuinely tight regime the S and P would not be one per cent off its high, and Singapore's exports would not be running at their fastest since nineteen eighty-eight. One of those two markets is wrong. We've sided with the bond market. We might be wrong.
Now — Singapore. Two bills, one barrel.

Within hours of each other on Tuesday, Singapore published its two biggest household-cost decisions of the quarter. Fares up seven per cent from Boxing Day. Electricity down ten point four per cent from today.
Same week, opposite directions.

Same energy shock, different calendars. The fare formula reads an energy index measured from July twenty-twenty-five to June twenty-twenty-six — the worst of the oil spike. The tariff reads gas prices from the first of July to the fifteenth of September, by which time they'd fallen.
So December bills a shock the October meter has already stopped registering.
Exactly that. And with Brent back near ninety-eight dollars, the relief has one quarter to run and the fare rise has no expiry at all.
[laughs] Somebody on HardwareZone got there before you, didn't they?
At one minute to one in the afternoon. A poster wrote — and I'm quoting — to make sinkies forget transport fare increase. Remember this is for one quarter while fares are permanent.
That's the whole page, written by a stranger.
That's the whole page. And here's the number underneath it. The formula permitted fourteen point seven per cent. The council granted seven. Which leaves seven point seven per cent still owed.
Owed meaning deferred to future years.
Deferred. And the unpaid overhang is now larger than what the formula generates in a whole year.
[thoughtful] So the rule has been suspended often enough that the backlog exceeds the rule.

We do, and it's ours. No. one-eighteen reported SP Group's quarterly tariff release as unpublished and overdue. It was neither. It went out on the twenty-ninth, the same calendar day as the two years before.
So why did we miss it?
[amused] Because it's served under an address reading first of July to thirtieth of September, twenty-twenty-seven. Wrong quarter, wrong year. The correctly-named address returns a not-found error.
Good. Own it and move on. Silicon.
Micron closed its fiscal year after the American market shut on Wednesday. Fourth-quarter revenue of fifty-four point two billion dollars, against eleven point three a year earlier.
[gasps] That's not growth, that's a different company.
Gross margin of eighty-six point eight per cent. Operating cash flow at eighty-one per cent of revenue.
What's the interesting part, if not the margin?
The contracts. Twenty-six signed long-term supply agreements carrying thirty-two billion dollars of customer commitments — the vast majority of it cash deposits. Running into twenty thirty-one.
And the Singapore line?

Buried in the prepared remarks. Cleanroom preparation at the high-bandwidth-memory packaging facility here is ahead of plan, with first output in early twenty twenty-seven. New York's fab makes its first wafer in twenty thirty.
So Singapore is inside the chain for the scarcest part in computing, three years before New York makes anything.
Which is the same story the port is telling. Electronic exports ran a hundred and thirty-one point eight per cent ahead of last August.
Home lab. This one made me wince.
A pull request against llama dot cpp. The idea: run the speculative-decoding draft head on the processor instead of the graphics card, so the draft cache comes off your video memory.
Which matters if your card is full.
On a twelve-gigabyte laptop card, baseline generation was twenty-eight point nine tokens a second. The hybrid mode gave fifty-five point two.
That's — what, ninety per cent faster?
Ninety-one. And using six hundred and thirty-eight fewer megabytes of video memory.
So where's the wince?
It was opened on Tuesday and closed, unmerged, the same day. Fifteen hours. The CUDA maintainer vetoed it on design grounds — backend-specific changes indicating too much technical debt.
Oh?

A tester running three cards on a dense model at very long context found the acceptance rate collapsing to twenty-two per cent, against a seventy-five to seventy-nine baseline. The author conceded he hadn't tested multiple GPUs.
So the ninety-one per cent was one card, one model, one rig.
And it did not survive contact with a second configuration. Which makes the veto look like judgement rather than gatekeeping.
The Kit — briefly, because the Atelier is the fun one today.

Two vendors put the same chip on sale a day apart. A hundred and ninety-two gigabytes of unified memory, up to a hundred and sixty of it handed to the graphics processor. Six and a half to seven and a half thousand dollars.
And how fast is it?
Nobody knows. No independent laboratory has measured either machine. The honest proxy, on last year's silicon, is about twenty-eight tokens a second averaged, eighteen at long context.
So you're buying capacity, not speed.
Capacity, and the fact that the weights never leave the house. We print no throughput figure for the new part, because nobody has measured one.
Good. Now — the Atelier. Torches.
[amused] Yes. And the headline is that the four-thousand-lumen claim is a thirty-second claim.
Meaning?
The standard measures output at thirty seconds. So a fifty-eight-gram light can honestly print four thousand two hundred lumens it physically cannot hold, because the heat has nowhere to go.
What should I ask for instead?
Candela. It's the number that tells you whether the beam actually reaches, and it's the one the marketing hides.
Give me the comparison.

A SureFire at two hundred and sixty-five dollars claims twelve hundred lumens and eleven thousand three hundred candela, publishes no colour rendering figure, and runs on disposable batteries. An Emisar at thirty-five dollars sixty-eight measures between two thousand three hundred and two thousand six hundred lumens, and eighteen to twenty thousand candela.
[scoffs] Seven times the price for half the light.

And there's a provenance problem. SureFire's product pages say Designed and Built in the USA. Its own education page explains that the illumination products cannot legally be marked Made in the USA — because, quote, we do import a few components, most notably the finest light-emitting diodes.
And the fair defence?
Regulation is real and worth buying once, around a hundred and forty dollars. Malkoff warrants for life. Though note — two American premium makers write the switch out of their warranties.
[warmly] Right. Take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
Freediving and spearfishing. And the thing that hooked me is that the technique and the physics fail at the same depth.
Around thirty metres. A diver with average lung proportions — six litres total, one and a half residual — reaches residual volume there. Below it the chest can't compress further without risk.
And the ears?

At almost exactly the same depth, the ordinary way of clearing them stops working. The pinch-and-blow method uses your breathing muscles to push air up. That works with a tank, horizontally. It doesn't work head-first on compressed lungs.
So the wall is the same wall.
The same wall. Which is why every third-level course in the sport is named after the manoeuvre that gets through it.
Tell me about the reflex, because I didn't know this.

You already have it. Submersion plus breath-hold triggers a slowed heart, narrowed peripheral vessels, and blood shifting into the chest. In one study, eighteen subjects holding for a mean of a hundred and thirty-seven seconds had their spleen volume fall twenty point eight per cent.
The spleen?
Squeezing stored red cells into circulation. Haemoglobin rose two point four per cent. And none of it happened when the same subjects rebreathed for the same length of time.
Okay. And the gear — because I know there's an argument.

The best one in the hobby. The settled community view is the opposite of the sales pitch. A competitor writing for a carbon-fin house said it was commonly said that the deeper you wanted to go, the stiffer your blades should be. That time is over.
Softer is better?

Softer allows smaller amplitude at higher frequency. Less drag, less oxygen. He went to a hundred and ten metres on medium blades and said his legs were killing him on the way up until he switched softer.
And what do the makers say you should actually spend on?
[laughs] The foot pocket. A hundred and ninety euro item. Both makers' buying guides converge on it — it does more for a diver than the blade bolted to it.
That's the least glamorous possible answer.
And here's my favourite thing on the page. The strongest argument against spending is made by the company charging the most.
Say more.

Alchemy's own writer, February last year: if you're a beginner, plastic fins are your best friend. Carbon fins are incredibly responsive, meaning they'll amplify both good and bad technique. If your kick is messy, carbon fins will punish you.
The eight-hundred-euro fin company says buy plastic.

And two days before this issue — three weeks after launching the most expensive fin of the year — the same author wrote that a product can be beautifully engineered, technologically advanced and completely unnecessary.
Give me the community numbers, because they were strange.

The world governing body has eleven videos on YouTube and nineteen and a half thousand subscribers. A competition photographer — not an athlete, not a federation — has four hundred and fifty-nine thousand.
[amused] The sport belongs to its artists.
And on the biggest spearfishing board, the speargun section has seventeen thousand posts, active this July. The safety section's most recent post is from November twenty twenty-two.
That's bleak.

The safety numbers are the hard part of this page. In depth competition, adverse events run at three to four per hundred dives. Across international team events from ninety-eight to two thousand and four, between nine point seven and eleven point one per cent of all performances were disqualified for signs of severe brain hypoxia.
And the danger isn't the bottom.
It's the last few metres and the surface. Oxygen partial pressure falls on the ascent, so the diver feels fine until he doesn't.
And the Singapore fact, which I loved.
The world's fastest-growing freediving agency is headquartered in Singapore. And under the Parks and Trees Act, merely carrying a hunting device in a marine park is an offence.
So the capital of breath-hold education —
— is a place where the water you train in is a swimming pool.
[laughs] Perfect. Culture and the body, quickly.
America's number one film at the weekend was seven years old. A re-release with new footage took twenty-six million dollars and beat three genuinely new wide openings.
And Tokyo?
Tokyo's number one was the detective reunion everyone is writing about. Two places below it sits a children's cartoon in its tenth week, on sixteen point eight billion yen.
So the nostalgia story is the smaller story.
By a factor of eight. And we owe a second correction there — we said that film opened at number one. It opened at number two and reached the top in its second weekend.
Noted. Watches?

No. one-eighteen flagged two irreconcilable prices for the revived Louis Vuitton Monterey. Nineteen thousand euros and twenty-three thousand. They reconcile. The gap is twenty-one per cent, which is Dutch value-added tax.
[chuckles] So not two prices. One price and a tax.
What we should have questioned instead was the movement. Forty-five hours of reserve, from a calibre developed for a different watch.
Family desk.

A study of one thousand three hundred and sixty-four adolescents put screen time and what children disclose online into the same model and let them compete. Time came out non-significant. Private online self-disclosure did not.
So it's not the hours.

It's what she tells strangers. But hold it loosely — the disclosure scale is three items, never validated, with an internal consistency coefficient of zero point five seven. And the average child in the study is fifteen.
Not twelve.
Not twelve. A finding centred on fifteen-year-olds is not a finding about a twelve-year-old, and the authors publish no breakdown for the younger ones.
And locally, the last PSLE paper was yesterday.
Yesterday. Which opens six weeks in which the honest answer is nothing. It's also the week the screen rationing ends.
Fitness, one line.
Seventeen cohorts, a hundred and seventy-six thousand participants. At around a hundred and fifty minutes a week, mortality ran about thirty-eight per cent lower. Then the curve flattens.
So more isn't more.

Past roughly seven and a half hours of brisk walking a week, you're buying something other than all-cause mortality. Every participant already had coronary heart disease, though — what transfers is the shape, not the number. Not medical advice.
And the diary date?

The fifth of December. Tickets open for the January sumo tournament in Tokyo — a chair seat is four to five and a half thousand yen. November's Fukuoka tournament is already sold out, all fifteen days.
[thoughtful] All right. The Undercurrent.

Pakistan. In February the electricity regulator ended net metering. The old arrangement let a household with panels export its daytime surplus and take back a unit at night, credited near retail — around twenty-five to twenty-seven rupees.
And the new one?
Imports charged at forty to sixty rupees. Exports bought at about ten to thirteen.
The intention being to stop the comfortable free-riding on a bankrupt grid.

Which was defensible. The tariff is stuffed with capacity payments — fixed, dollar-indexed obligations that make up eighty-two per cent of what a consumer pays. Every household that stops buying leaves that bill to be split among fewer units.
So what actually happened?

The government's own economists published it four months later, without euphemism. When a prosumer stores surplus electricity rather than exporting it, each stored unit displaces an imported unit worth forty to fifty-five rupees instead of earning eleven.
[pause] So the rule made a battery four times more valuable than the cable.
Lithium storage imports hit four point six gigawatt-hours in twenty twenty-five alone. Sixty per cent of everything imported since twenty eighteen, in one year.
And the grid?

Grid sales fell from a hundred and twenty-five terawatt-hours to a hundred and eleven in three years, while the number of customers grew. National demand fell eight point six six per cent last financial year.
When the Strait closed in April, the official grid lost up to five thousand megawatts overnight and load-shedding came back. And the households with panels and batteries didn't notice.
Official installed capacity is forty-one gigawatts. Add the solar the state does not count and it's about seventy-nine.
So there's a second power system nobody measures.

And nobody agrees on its size. The minister says twenty-two gigawatts. A think tank says thirty-eight. Another count says thirty-one. As a researcher there put it — we are making billion-rupee decisions based on data that misses nearly half.
And who loses?

The people who cannot leave. A man on the second floor inside Mochi Gate in Lahore told a reporter that his brother has built a cage for pigeons on the roof, there are tall buildings on both sides, and very little direct sunlight reaches. So panels cannot be installed, and he can see no alternative.
[thoughtful] Nearly one in five Pakistani homes has solar. Only one in twenty-six of those has a battery.
It is drafting a national battery framework, and an adviser has proposed paying households eighteen to twenty-two rupees a unit to discharge their own batteries back into the grid at dusk.
[drawn out] More than it pays them for the daytime export.
Having failed to keep its customers as customers, it proposes to become their tenant.
And the honest caveat?

The grid was dying before the batteries arrived. Net billing saves about thirty-two billion rupees against a circular debt of one point eight trillion. The batteries are an accelerant on a fire lit by take-or-pay contracts and forty per cent collection rates.
So the right sentence isn't batteries are killing the grid.
It's that batteries have made it impossible to fix by the only instrument the state has. Which is the tariff.
[thoughtful] And why does a listener here care?

Because Singapore is building its energy future on the opposite bet. Imported power, a regional grid, a tariff set centrally. And the cost curve that broke the Pakistani settlement is not a Pakistani curve.
It's arriving everywhere.
It's arriving everywhere. And it asks a question no regulator has answered — what a utility is for, once its best customers can generate and store more cheaply than it can bill them.
[pause] That's a good place to stop.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
